abstract: Atalay studies how occupational exposure to AI relates to wages across 671 US occupations, combining occupation-level wage data with an AI exposure index. Cross-sectional regressions with robust standard errors, controlling for employment size and occupational characteristics, find a positive and statistically significant association: more-exposed occupations have higher wages. The pattern holds across specifications and across the wage distribution in quantile regressions. It is broadly robust to an instrumental-variable approach and stronger in occupations with higher cognitive skill intensity. The author notes that occupational skill composition explains part of the relationship, while a residual association remains. The full text was not accessible, so no coefficient sizes are recorded here.
keyFindings: Across 671 US occupations, AI exposure is positively and significantly associated with wage levels
The association holds across model specifications and across the wage distribution (quantile regression), and is broadly consistent under an instrumental-variable approach
The association is stronger in occupations with higher cognitive skill intensity
Occupational skill composition explains part of the exposure–wage relationship; a residual association remains
methodology: Occupation-level cross-section of 671 US occupations; wage data combined with an AI exposure index (potential exposure). OLS with robust standard errors, controls for employment size and occupational characteristics; quantile regressions; instrumental-variable robustness check. Data years and exposure index not confirmed (full text inaccessible).
qualifiers: Tier 1: peer-reviewed (Journal of Economic Studies, Emerald). Cross-sectional association, not a causal wage effect of AI: high-exposure occupations were already high-wage cognitive jobs, and the author concedes that skill composition explains part of the link. Occupation-level data miss within-occupation wage variation. The exposure index measures potential exposure, not firm-level adoption (the author's own stated limitation). Coefficients not verified: only the publisher abstract was read.
